screens.title: Inheritance: Building Hierarchies
screens.subtitle: How derived classes reuse and specialize base class behavior in C++

narration.text: In this lesson we explore inheritance, the mechanism that lets us create a new class from an existing one and express natural 'is-a' relationships. You'll learn how a derived class reuses attributes and behaviors from a base class, how access modes affect visibility, and why constructor and destructor order matter for correct initialization and cleanup. We'll use a Vehicle and Car example to make ideas concrete, and later you'll implement a Shape and Circle to practice constructor chaining and method overriding. By the end, you should be able to decide when inheritance is appropriate and when composition is the clearer design. A common pitfall we'll guard against is using inheritance to express 'has-a' relationships — that often leads to brittle or confusing hierarchies. Throughout the lesson I'll point out practical checks you can use when designing classes, show how to call base class functions from overridden methods, and explain how protected members let derived classes access implementation details without exposing them publicly. Think about a Car and a Vehicle: when does it make sense for Car to inherit from Vehicle, and when does it make more sense for Car to contain another object? Keep that question in mind as we proceed; it will help you form better designs.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Inheritance expresses an 'is-a' relationship so derived classes reuse and extend base class state and behavior; access modes and constructor/destructor order control how that reuse is exposed and performed.

Inheritance: Building Hierarchies

Understand how derived classes reuse base class behavior, affect visibility, and how constructors and destructors run across a hierarchy.

Duration: ~11 minutes
In this lesson
Learn the is-a relationship and constructor chaining.
Coming up

Practice

Example snippet
#include <iostream>
class Vehicle { /* speed, color, accelerate, brake */ };
class Car : public Vehicle { /* numDoors, startEngine, override displayInfo */ };
Why it matters

Inheritance reduces duplication and models natural taxonomies. Correct use prevents maintenance problems and preserves encapsulation.

Key Takeaway

Treat inheritance as a precise semantic relationship. If you cannot truthfully answer 'is a' then prefer composition.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives give you a clear map of skills to practice as you study inheritance. You'll start by understanding the concept itself and why we model relationships with inheritance. Then you'll be able to distinguish base and derived classes and state the 'is-a' relationship confidently. Next, you'll implement single inheritance in real C++ code and choose the right access mode so members keep their intended visibility. Finally, you will be able to explain constructor chaining and destructor order at runtime. Each objective is connected to a concrete coding action: reading and tracing constructors, writing derived class definitions using an initializer list, and observing output when creating and destroying objects. The exercises that follow will make these skills mechanical: you will write a Circle derived from Shape, validate inputs, and override a method correctly. As you work, ask whether a candidate relationship is truly 'is-a' or better expressed via composition — that question will guide your design decisions and prevent common architecture mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Skill focus
keyIdea.text: Combine conceptual understanding with practical coding: implement inheritance correctly, manage visibility, and reason about initialization order.

You'll practice method overriding so a derived class can specialize behavior and still call the base implementation when appropriate. You'll identify and correct common mistakes, like using inheritance to represent 'has-a' relationships or forgetting to call a base class constructor when it has no default. screens.title: What is inheritance?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role, and a concrete Vehicle → Car example

narration.text: Inheritance is an object-oriented mechanism that lets you define a new class based on an existing one so the new class automatically gets the base class's data members and member functions. In practical terms this promotes code reuse: rather than copying methods into a new class, you derive that class from an existing implementation. A common everyday example is Vehicle and Car. Vehicle provides general properties like speed and color and behaviors like accelerate and brake. Car inherits those features and adds its own field such as number of doors or a startEngine method. The derived class can also override a base method to provide a more specific implementation; for instance Car might override a displayInfo method to include the number of doors while still using the base display logic. A misconception is to assume inheritance always reduces complexity — if the relationship is not truly 'is-a' you will create confusing coupling. Another subtle point is that inheriting members' visibility depends on access mode; protected members are visible to derived classes but hidden from external code, which allows careful sharing of implementation without exposing it as a public A P I. After you can state this definition and give the Vehicle/Car example, you are ready to explore access modes and initialization order.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance creates a subtype relationship where derived classes reuse and can specialize base class behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is inheritance?
Definition

Inheritance in one sentence

A derived class reuses the data and behavior of a base class and can extend or override it.

Key bullets
  • Promotes code reuse and logical modeling.
  • Base class is parent; derived class is child.
  • Protected members accessible to derived classes.
  • Choose inheritance only for true subtype relationships.
Key Takeaway

Use inheritance to model 'is-a' relationships and keep implementation details hidden via access control.

Example
Vehicle (base)
protected: color, speed • public: accelerate(), brake(), displayInfo()
Car : public Vehicle (derived)
private: numDoors • public: startEngine(), overridden displayInfo()
Common misconception

Do not use inheritance to model 'has-a' relationships such as Car inheriting from Engine. Composition is the correct design for ownership or usage relationships.

When to inherit
If the derived object truly is a kind of the base object.
When to avoid
If you only need access to functionality, prefer a member object instead of inheritance.

narration.text: Understanding the roles of base and derived classes helps you design clearer hierarchies. The base class defines general state and behavior shared by many types; it provides a common interface and can hold protected members to share implementation with derived classes. The derived class specializes or extends those general behaviors. For example, Vehicle describes speed and methods to accelerate and brake. Car, a derived type, reuses those behaviors and adds fields like number of doors and methods like startEngine. A practical design check is to ask whether every candidate derived object can stand in for its base — that is, can you use a Car wherever a Vehicle is expected? If yes, inheritance is appropriate. Another contrast is access: public inheritance preserves public and protected visibility, protected inheritance downgrades public to protected and private inheritance hides them from external code by making them private in the derived type. A common mistake is to assume protected equals public; protected members are accessible to derived classes but still hidden from other code. Consider testing your design by writing small example code that declares a base pointer to a derived object and calls base methods; if that passes semantic checks, your 'is-a' relationship is likely valid.

keyIdea.title: Role contrast
keyIdea.text: Base classes express common behavior; derived classes specialize. Use the 'substitutability' check: can derived stand in for base?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Base vs Derived
Base Class
Vehicle
  • Defines shared data: color, speed.
  • Defines behaviors: accelerate, brake, displayInfo.
  • Can expose protected members to derived classes.
Design tip: keep stable API in base classes to avoid breaking derived types.
Derived Class
Car : public Vehicle
  • Adds specific data: numDoors.
  • Specializes behavior: startEngine, override displayInfo.
  • Can call base methods using scope resolution.
Practical check: if you need a Car object where a Vehicle is expected, inheritance is correct.
Substitutability
Can the derived object be used in place of the base type?
Visibility
public/protected/private inheritance affect how inherited members are exposed.
Design smell
Inheriting for code reuse rather than logical taxonomy often indicates a design smell.

screens.title: public, protected, private inheritance
screens.subtitle: How access modes change member visibility in a derived class

narration.text: C++ lets you choose how a derived class inherits the accessibility of base members using public, protected, or private inheritance. With public inheritance, the simplest and most common mode, public members remain public and protected members remain protected in the derived class; this preserves the base class interface for users of the derived type. Protected inheritance changes both public and protected members into protected members in the derived class, making them accessible only to the derived class and its subclasses but not to external callers. Private inheritance makes public and protected base members private in the derived class, hiding them from outside code entirely; this is rarely used to model a 'has-a' relationship via implementation inheritance. A useful concrete check: if a base class provides a public method and you inherit publicly, code using a derived object can still call that method. If you inherit privately, that same call will fail because the method becomes private. A common misconception is that inheritance visibility affects the base class itself — it does not. It only alters how the derived class exposes the inherited members. Keep these rules in mind when choosing the inheritance mode to preserve the expected public A P I.

keyIdea.title: Visibility rules
keyIdea.text: Public preserves interface, protected restricts to derivation, private hides inherited members from outside code.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Access Modes
Rules
public
public -> public, protected -> protected. Preserves interface and is the usual mode.
protected
public & protected become protected. Useful to hide interface from external callers but keep for subclasses.
private
public & protected become private. Inherited members hidden from outside—rarely used for 'is-a'.
Concrete example
// If Vehicle::displayInfo() is public:
class Car : public Vehicle { /* Car can be used where Vehicle is expected */ };
class SecretCar : private Vehicle { /* Vehicle methods become private in SecretCar */ };
Misconception

The access mode does not change the base class itself. It only changes how the derived class exposes the inherited members.

Quick checks
  • Do you need external code to call base methods via derived objects? Use public.
  • Do you only want derived classes to access base methods? Consider protected.
  • Do you want to reuse implementation but hide interface? Prefer composition over private inheritance.

screens.title: Constructor chaining and initializer lists
screens.subtitle: How base and derived constructors run and how to call base constructors

narration.text: Constructor chaining is the process by which constructors run from the base classes up to the most derived class during object creation. In C++ the base class constructor is always called before the derived class constructor. This guarantees the base portion of the object is properly initialized before derived-specific initialization runs. To pass arguments to a non-default base constructor you must call it explicitly in the derived constructor's initializer list; for example Car(std::string c, double s, int doors) : Vehicle(c, s), numDoors(doors) calls Vehicle's constructor first, then initializes numDoors, and finally executes the Car constructor body. If the base class has only parameterized constructors and you do not call one, the code fails to compile because there is no default constructor to call. A common mistake is to attempt to assign base members inside the derived constructor body instead of using initializer lists; that can lead to extra work or missed initialization for const or reference members. As a practical exercise, write small programs printing constructor messages to observe the order and confirm that base constructors run before derived constructors.

keyIdea.title: Constructor rule
keyIdea.text: Base constructors run first. Use initializer lists to forward arguments and ensure correct initialization.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Constructor chaining
Process
  1. Allocate object memory for derived type.
  2. Call base class constructors (most base first).
  3. Initialize derived members using initializer list.
  4. Execute derived constructor body.
Example initializer list
Car(std::string c, double s, int doors) : Vehicle(c, s), numDoors(doors) { std::cout << "Car constructor" << std::endl; }
Why initializer lists matter
  • Directly construct base subobject with correct arguments.
  • Avoids assignment after default construction, which can be inefficient.
  • Required for const and reference members that cannot be assigned later.
Try this
Add cout messages to Shape and Circle constructors to observe call order when creating a Circle.

screens.title: Destructor order and resource cleanup
screens.subtitle: Why derived destructors run first and how that prevents resource leaks

narration.text: Destructors run in the reverse order of constructors: the most derived destructor executes first, then the base destructors unwind back to the most base class. This reverse ordering ensures that derived-specific resources are released before base-class cleanup runs. Consider a derived class that allocates memory or holds handles to external resources; calling the derived destructor first is necessary so those resources are freed while derived-specific state is still valid. After the derived destructor finishes, the base destructor runs to clean up the base portion of the object. A common confusion is thinking destructors run in the same order as constructors — they do not. To observe this, instrument constructors and destructors with print statements; when you create and then destroy an object, you'll see base constructors run first and derived destructors run first. This understanding is crucial for correct RAII usage and for writing safe destructors when polymorphism is involved. Remember to make destructors virtual in a base class if you plan to delete derived objects via base pointers so the derived destructor runs properly. Destructor order and resource cleanup means destructors run derived-first, base-last. make base destructors virtual when deleting through base pointers.. In practical terms, why derived destructors run first and how that prevents resource leaks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Destructor rule
keyIdea.text: Destructors run derived-first, base-last. Make base destructors virtual when deleting through base pointers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Destructor order
Observation

Constructors go base→derived. Destructors go derived→base. This pattern protects derived resources during teardown.

Example output
Vehicle constructor called.
Car constructor called.
Car destructor called.
Vehicle destructor called.
Polymorphism note
If you delete derived objects through base pointers, make the base destructor virtual so the derived destructor runs.
Common mistake
Omitting virtual destructor in base classes can silently skip derived cleanup when deleting via base pointers.
Key Takeaway

Destructor order protects derived cleanup. Use virtual destructors for polymorphic base classes.

screens.title: Method overriding and calling base implementations
screens.subtitle: Override displayInfo() in Car and call Vehicle::displayInfo()

narration.text: Method overriding lets a derived class provide its own implementation for a function already defined in the base class. In our Vehicle and Car example, Vehicle defines displayInfo to print color and speed. Car overrides displayInfo to include number of doors. When overriding, you can still call the base version from the derived method using the scope resolution operator, for example Vehicle::displayInfo(); this is useful to reuse base behavior and then append derived-specific details. A common misunderstanding is to expect the base version to run automatically when the derived method executes — it does not; you must call it explicitly if you want its effects. Another point is that overriding in C++ requires the derived method to have the same signature; if you intend polymorphic behavior through base pointers, mark the base method virtual. Below is a concrete code example illustrating override and explicit call to the base display method. Try compiling and running the snippet to observe that Car's displayInfo prints the base information then the derived information, demonstrating deliberate reuse rather than accidental duplication. Method overriding and calling base implementations means derived methods replace base implementations; call the base version explicitly when you want to reuse its behavior.. In practical terms, override displayinfo() in car and call vehicle::displayinfo(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Override rule
keyIdea.text: Derived methods replace base implementations; call the base version explicitly when you want to reuse its behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Method overriding
Code example
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Vehicle {
public:
  Vehicle(std::string c, double s) : color(c), speed(s) {}
  void displayInfo() const {
    std::cout << "Color: " << color << ", Speed: " << speed << " km/h" << std::endl;
  }
protected:
  std::string color;
  double speed;
};

class Car : public Vehicle {
private:
  int numDoors;
public:
  Car(std::string c, double s, int d) : Vehicle(c, s), numDoors(d) {}
  void displayInfo() const {              // override (not virtual in this example)
    Vehicle::displayInfo();               // call base implementation
    std::cout << "Number of doors: " << numDoors << std::endl;
  }
};

int main() {
  Car myCar("Red", 60.0, 4);
  myCar.displayInfo();
  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • Car defines its own displayInfo with the same signature as Vehicle.
  • Vehicle::displayInfo is explicitly called to reuse base behavior.
  • To enable polymorphic calls through base pointers, declare Vehicle::displayInfo as virtual.
Misconception
Overriding does not implicitly call the base version; you must call it if needed.
Key Takeaway

Use overriding to specialize behavior; explicitly call the base version to compose behaviors.

screens.title: Protected members and derived access
screens.subtitle: What protected means and why it exists

narration.text: Protected members sit between public and private: they are part of the class's implementation but are accessible to derived classes. A protected data member like color in the Vehicle example allows derived classes such as Car to read and modify it without exposing it to external code that uses a Vehicle or Car object. That capability is useful when derived types need to build on base state. However, protected members are not an excuse to make everything broadly visible; they couple derived classes to base implementation, so use them sparingly. If you want to expose a stable interface to users while allowing controlled extension, prefer protected for internals that derived types legitimately need, and keep other members private with public getters or setters when you want to limit direct access. A common misconception is to treat protected as public — remember it is still hidden from outside code. If many derived classes require different aspects of base state, consider providing protected helper functions instead of exposing raw data. This preserves invariants and gives you a single place to change behavior later.

keyIdea.title: Protected role
keyIdea.text: Protected allows derived classes access to implementation details without exposing them to external callers; use it judiciously.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Protected members
What protected gives you

Protected members allow derived classes to access internal state while keeping that state hidden from external users of the class.

Vehicle
protected: color, speed — accessible to Car but not to main()
Best practice
Prefer protected helper functions over exposing raw protected data widely.
Misuse
Treating protected members as part of a public API couples derived types to implementation details.
Concrete tip

If multiple derived classes need a transformation, expose a protected method in the base class that performs it rather than exposing the underlying data directly.

Check your design

Would a small protected helper reduce repetition while preserving encapsulation? If so, prefer the helper.

narration.text: A frequent design question is whether to model a relationship with inheritance or composition. Composition means one class contains another as a member — for example a Car has an Engine. Inheritance would be inappropriate there because a Car is not a kind of Engine. Use composition when you want to encapsulate a reusable component or when you want to change behavior by swapping member objects at runtime. In contrast, inheritance models a subtype: a Car is a Vehicle. Composition leads to clearer ownership semantics and usually less coupling between class interfaces. A typical mistake is to inherit purely for convenience to reuse code from another class; that tends to expose implementation details and breaks substitutability. When in doubt, ask whether the derived object truly satisfies the semantics of being a base object. If the relationship is primarily about reusing code or sharing internal helpers, prefer composition or refactor shared code into helper classes or functions. This approach leads to more maintainable and flexible designs over time. Composition vs Inheritance means prefer composition ('has-a') for ownership and flexible behavior; use inheritance ('is-a') for true subtype relationships.. In practical terms, when to use 'has-a' (composition) instead of 'is-a' (inheritance). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design choice
keyIdea.text: Prefer composition ('has-a') for ownership and flexible behavior; use inheritance ('is-a') for true subtype relationships.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Composition vs Inheritance
Composition (has-a)
  • Car has an Engine as a member.
  • Ownership and lifetimes are clearer.
  • Swap components to change behavior at runtime.
Inheritance (is-a)
  • Car is a Vehicle — it can be used where Vehicle is expected.
  • Enables polymorphism when base methods are virtual.
  • Should model true subtype relationships only.
Rule of thumb
If you cannot truthfully say Derived is a Base, prefer composition.
Refactor tip
Extract shared code into helper classes rather than using inheritance for reuse.
Design smell
Multiple unrelated responsibilities in a base class indicate poor abstraction for inheritance.

screens.title: Shape and Circle: implement the supplied exercise
screens.subtitle: Complete the Circle class: validate radius, override displayColor, and observe constructor/destructor order

narration.text: Now we work through the hands-on Shape/Circle exercise from the chapter. The Shape base class holds a protected color string and prints constructor and destructor messages. Circle derives publicly from Shape and must initialize the base color using an initializer list. It must also validate radius: if the supplied radius is not positive, set it to a default positive value and print a message. Circle should override displayColor to call the base Shape::displayColor and then print radius. A clear pattern is to use the initializer list to call Shape(c) and initialize radius in the same list; then the constructor body can perform validation logic. Also include destructor messages in both classes so you can observe destruction order by creating and destroying Circle objects in main. This task ties together constructor chaining, access to protected members, method overriding with explicit base calls, and simple input validation. Implement the Circle methods, run the program, and confirm that the output shows Shape constructor first, Circle constructor next, then on program end Circle destructor then Shape destructor. Shape and Circle: implement the supplied exercise means use initializer lists and override methods while validating inputs; observe constructor/destructor order via printed messages.. In practical terms, complete the circle class: validate radius, override displaycolor, and observe constructor/destructor order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use initializer lists and override methods while validating inputs; observe constructor/destructor order via printed messages.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Shape → Circle Activity
Starter code
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cmath>

class Shape {
protected:
  std::string color;
public:
  Shape(std::string c) : color(c) {
    std::cout << "Shape constructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
  void displayColor() const {
    std::cout << "Shape Color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
  ~Shape() {
    std::cout << "Shape destructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
};

class Circle : public Shape {
private:
  double radius;
public:
  Circle(std::string c, double r) : Shape(c) { /* initialize radius with validation */ }
  double getArea() const { /* return area */ }
  void displayColor() const { /* call Shape::displayColor and print radius */ }
  ~Circle() { std::cout << "Circle destructor called with radius: " << radius << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
  Circle myCircle("Blue", 5.0);
  myCircle.displayColor();
  std::cout << "Circle Area: " << myCircle.getArea() << std::endl;
  Circle invalidCircle("Red", -2.0);
  invalidCircle.displayColor();
  return 0;
}
Implementation hints
Use initializer list to call Shape(c) and initialize radius. Validate radius > 0 or set to 1.0 and print a message.
Test checklist
Observe constructor/destructor messages. Confirm displayColor prints both color and radius. Check getArea computes pi * r * r.
Key Takeaway

This exercise combines initializer lists, overriding, validation, and lifecycle observation to reinforce inheritance mechanics.

screens.title: Complete Circle implementation (reference)
screens.subtitle: A correct Circle constructor, getArea, and overridden displayColor

narration.text: Here is a reference implementation that follows the chapter's requirements. The Circle constructor calls Shape(c) in the initializer list and initializes radius. It validates radius in the constructor body so negative values are handled gracefully. The getArea method computes the area using pi and radius, and displayColor overrides Shape::displayColor by calling Shape::displayColor and then printing the radius. Destructors print messages so you can confirm the destructor ordering in practice. Study this implementation to see how initializer lists, validation, and explicit base calls combine in a simple derived class. A common beginner error is to forget to initialize radius before printing it in the constructor body; the initializer list ensures predictable initialization. Use this implementation as a template, then experiment by making radius a const or a reference to see how initializer lists become mandatory for those cases. Complete Circle implementation (reference) means initializer lists plus explicit base calls produce safe, readable derived class initialization and behavior.. In practical terms, a correct circle constructor, getarea, and overridden displaycolor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Circle: Reference Solution
Reference code
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cmath>

class Shape {
protected:
  std::string color;
public:
  Shape(std::string c) : color(c) {
    std::cout << "Shape constructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
  void displayColor() const {
    std::cout << "Shape Color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
  ~Shape() {
    std::cout << "Shape destructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
  }
};

class Circle : public Shape {
private:
  double radius;
public:
  Circle(std::string c, double r) : Shape(c), radius(r) {
    if (radius <= 0) {
      std::cout << "Invalid radius, setting to 1.0" << std::endl;
      radius = 1.0;
    }
    std::cout << "Circle constructor called with radius: " << radius << std::endl;
  }

  double getArea() const {
    return M_PI * radius * radius;
  }

  void displayColor() const {
    Shape::displayColor();
    std::cout << "Radius: " << radius << std::endl;
  }

  ~Circle() {
    std::cout << "Circle destructor called with radius: " << radius << std::endl;
  }
};

int main() {
  Circle myCircle("Blue", 5.0);
  myCircle.displayColor();
  std::cout << "Circle Area: " << myCircle.getArea() << std::endl;

  Circle invalidCircle("Red", -2.0);
  invalidCircle.displayColor();
  return 0;
}
Why this works
Initializer list constructs Shape subobject and radius before constructor body runs, ensuring safe use of members.
Validation
Validation happens in the constructor body after initialization so you can adjust invalid values deterministically.

screens.title: Common errors and best practices
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to avoid compilation and design bugs

narration.text: As you apply inheritance, watch for several recurring errors. First, forgetting to call a non-default base constructor in the derived initializer list causes compilation failure; always forward required arguments. Second, omitting virtual destructors in base classes when you plan polymorphic deletion can skip derived cleanup, leading to resource leaks. Third, using private inheritance to hide an interface when composition would be clearer often results in fragile code; prefer composition for implementation reuse. Fourth, overusing protected data exposes implementation details and couples derived classes to base internals; prefer protected helper functions or private data with public accessors. Fifth, overriding with a mismatched signature silently hides the base method rather than overriding it; ensure signatures match or mark base methods virtual and add override on derived methods when possible to catch errors. Finally, when designing a hierarchy, apply the substitutability check: if a derived type cannot be used wherever the base is expected, do not inherit. These rules reduce surprises and make hierarchies easier to maintain. Common mistakes
  • Not calling required base constructors in initializer list.
  • Missing virtual destructor in polymorphic base classes.
  • Using inheritance for 'has-a' relationships instead of composition.
  • Overexposing protected data and creating tight coupling.
Best practices
  • Prefer public inheritance for true subtypes.
  • Use initializer lists for predictable initialization.
  • Mark base methods virtual when polymorphism is intended and use override in derived methods.
  • Prefer composition when the relationship is not subtype.
Check before you inherit
Can you substitute the derived type everywhere the base is used? If not, choose composition.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the main concepts to carry forward. First, inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship: derived classes reuse and specialize base class behavior. Second, access modes — public, protected, private — determine how inherited members are exposed in the derived class and must be chosen to preserve intended interfaces. Third, constructor chaining runs from base to derived while destructors run from derived to base; use initializer lists to forward arguments to base constructors. Fourth, method overriding lets derived classes provide specific behavior and you can call the base implementation explicitly using the scope resolution operator. Fifth, protect resources by making base destructors virtual when you delete through base pointers. Lastly, prefer composition for 'has-a' relationships and avoid inheritance purely for code reuse. Keep these points in mind as quick design checks when building class hierarchies.
